content.thinking:
I need to draft the root cause, executive summary, and assumptions carefully, noting that the error rate actually declined slightly while latency was the real impact, so I should avoid overstating figures already computed. I should flag clearly that the deploy-as-cause link rests on timing correlation rather than direct evidence, that attributing ClientDisconnected errors to slow renders is an inference, and that the recovery being tied to the rollback is uncertain given the short observation window.

I'm also noting the timing discrepancy: recovery was marked at 15:40 just seconds after the rollback at 15:39:55, so crediting the rollback for recovery this fast is speculative. Similarly, since ClientDisconnected errors surfaced at 15:33, before the deploy or incident onset, that undermines a clean causal story and needs to be called out as an inconsistency rather than smoothed over.

assumptions: The deploy is linked to the slowdown by timing and by code reading, not by profiling or tracing of the running service; no direct measurement of time spent in average_spend_per_item was collected.

Recovery is attributed to the rollback because the service returned to baseline shortly after it, but the rollback and the observed recovery are only about twelve seconds apart, so the causal link is inferred rather than demonstrated.

The 'ClientDisconnected' log errors are assumed to be shoppers abandoning slow page loads. They are not proof of that, and they appear from 15:33 onward — a minute before the deploy and the onset — so at least some of them have another explanation.

Customer impact is inferred from latency and disconnect logs. The error rate during the window was not above the preceding baseline, so no measured increase in failed requests supports the impact claim.
The size of the affected population is not known; the O(n^2) behaviour would hurt accounts with many purchases most, but no breakdown by account size was gathered.

Only io-shop's own metrics, logs and change events were examined, over a limited lookback. No upstream or downstream service was checked, so a contributing factor outside this service was not ruled out.
The proposed fix in the draft pull request has not been tested or verified against this incident.
input.executive_summary: A code change released at 15:34 UTC on 27 September 2026 made the customer account page far slower to load. Pages that had previously rendered in a fraction of a second took several seconds for customers with longer purchase histories, and some shoppers gave up and closed the page before it finished loading. The slowdown lasted about six minutes, from 15:34 until metrics returned to normal at 15:40, and affected shoppers viewing their account pages; ordering and other parts of the shop were not implicated. Automated monitoring raised a latency alert at 15:39, an automated responder identified the release as the likely cause within roughly half a minute, and the release was rolled back at 15:39:55, after which the service returned to its normal performance. A draft pull request has been opened to correct the inefficient calculation before the change is re-released. Note that the overall share of failed requests during the window was not higher than the period before the incident — the measured impact was slow page loads rather than a rise in outright failures.
input.root_cause: A deploy of io-shop at 15:34:00Z (revision 5e07d73148d0a704b8fefe5f379bc652bb773655) replaced a constant-time average calculation (account.total_cents // len(purchases)) in average_spend_per_item with a nested loop that recomputes the running purchase sum on each iteration, making the account-page render path O(n^2) in the number of purchases. Latency across p50/p95/p99 jumped in the same minute the deploy landed while request volume and CPU/memory stayed flat, and rolling the deploy back returned the service to baseline.
